title: Super-Precise Latency: code and analysis for the effect of CPU threading on high-precision latency, and an industry-wide audit

creators.name: Ricou, Gustavo Pedro
creators.affiliation: School of Computer Science and Statistics, Trinity College Dublin, Dublin, Ireland

creators.name: Duvignau, Romaric
creators.affiliation: Department of Computer Science and Engineering, Chalmers University of Technology, Gothenburg, Sweden

description:
Code, analysis and manuscript for Super-Precise Latency: How CPU Threading Affects High-Precision Latency, and an Industry-Wide Audit. Message-broker benchmarks now report latencies below a millisecond, shorter than a thread can wait for a processor core before it reads the clock.

The distribution and the mechanism. After a broker writes a message it acknowledges it to the producer and delivers it to the consumer; read on one machine and one clock, the two readings should coincide. Their difference spreads over milliseconds and falls below zero for 62,264 of 738,730 messages, while no latency timed from the publish call does. The cause is scheduling: the thread that reads the acknowledgment can wait for a core longer than the message takes to reach the consumer. The rate is the thread's waiting probability times the chance that its residual wait outlasts the end-to-end latency, on the timescale of the scheduler's base slice; real-time priority for the threads that read the clock, at unchanged utilization, cut the rate 7 to 80 times, and a kernel trace predicts it with nothing fitted.

The industry-wide audit. Seven of ten measurement tools read at source dispose of a latency at or below zero without counting it, by filtering it, letting a library refuse it or substituting another value; ten of eleven benchmarking tools run under registered predictions take both timestamps in one process and cannot measure a one-way latency. A positivity filter on a millisecond clock also deletes the fastest messages: in 71 of 75 settings the benchmark measured in depth printed a median of exactly 1.0 or 2.0 ms, computed from as little as 0.36% of its samples, and none of 43 public reports states how many samples it kept. The paper gives checks for benchmark authors and readers, and measures what each buys.

What changed in v4.0. On 5 October 2026 the paper was rebuilt around four bottom lines (the distribution, the mechanism and its laws, the industry-wide audit, and what to do) under the title above, and the supplement was cut to the evidence those need; the earlier paper and supplement are kept in docs/archive/2026-10-05-before-cleanup. Before that, an outside editor's review of v3, taken whole. (1) The paper was rewritten under the title Faster than Light: Silent Errors in the Latency Benchmarks Used to Choose Message Brokers: two failures given equal space, the claim before its concessions, one name per thing, and fifteen pointers into the supplement where there were forty-six; it was then organized around its three parts, the finding, its mechanism and how the industry handles it, with the practical implications leading the abstract and the introduction and set out in a section of their own. (2) The reach of the deletion was tested, not assumed: an audit of 43 published reports, registered before any was read (freezes/29), found the signature fixed in advance in eight configurations of two reports and a stated retention in none. (3) The supplement became two documents: supplement.pdf, the supplementary material, organized by the paper's sections; and postmortem.pdf, the complete single-author record of how the results were obtained, which is not part of the submission. (4) The registered law campaign on three Microsoft Azure pairs is reported in full: one prediction confirmed on every campaign that tested it, three on one broker, the rest not. (5) Errors found and corrected, each against its data: the sign check rejects 109 of the 126 runs behind our first result and every one of its six conditions, not every run; the end-to-end latency is defined to the time the consumer has handled the record, as it was always computed; the transport replication fails the criterion registered for it, by under a hundredth of a millisecond; E-A7's registered occupancy fall did not happen; the grid-membership test was built after its campaign; the workstation testbed runs under a hypervisor. Every number in the three documents is recomputed from the committed data by the archived code, and the tests fail if text and data disagree.

What changed in v3.0. Two more authors, and the model at the centre of Mode A became an identity. (1) The creator list grew to four, which is why this was a major version. R. Duvignau joined on a correction that changed the work rather than the wording: the broker's append precedes both the producer's acknowledgment and the consumer's receipt while neither precedes the other, so there is no happens-before relation for a negative span to violate. Two further authors joined at this version and have since withdrawn — one on his own standard for taking public responsibility for a deposited record he has not audited, one on an objection to how the work was produced — and neither is named on this record. The corrections they contributed stand, including the rule that a load generator must be verified rather than assumed, which is one of the reporting rules the paper ends with. (2) Section III's model is an identity, not a fit. S = D − A per event, stated assuming no ordering, with Pr[S < 0] = Pr[A > D] following from it; both sides are recounted from the committed corpus on every build and the build fails if they part. The residual of the Time-to-Insight decomposition is named as the acknowledgment lag the harness stamps, rather than an unobserved append-to-deliver delay nothing measures. (3) The two-broker gap is measured on workloads that match: a paired 1.7× over matched conditions, with a fifth of the pairs running the other way. (4) A fifth timestamp is named and bounded. The two clients deserialize on opposite sides of the receive stamp, so every span referenced to it carries one client's payload parse and not the other's — 281 ns against 19,480 ns at the median. (5) The source audit grows from five instrumentation tools to ten, and records that a search for any stated defence of the positivity guard came back empty. (6) New gates, each demonstrated failing on the defect it guards before that defect was repaired: claim-to-equation agreement, float labelling, figure reading rules, cross-sentence dependency, per-corpus denominators, front matter checked against the BUILT PDF rather than the source, and a cross-reference rule that fails any pointer resolving to an empty number. 4,175 tests at 100% branch coverage, up from 3,866. (7) The supplement's title page, unchanged since round 4, carried one author under a title the paper does not have; it now carries the paper's title, the byline and a running head on every page. The manuscript holds at twelve pages, five figures, two tables and 44 of 45 permitted references, with the displaced material in a supplement that grew from 49 pages to 54.

What changed in v2.7. A co-author, a title, and the first sustained pass at explaining the system before making claims about it. (1) An author joined who has since withdrawn, and the record takes the manuscript's new title — both of which this record had wrong until now. (2) The system is drawn before any claim is made about it: a figure inside the first two pages showing which threads do the benchmark's work, which record times, and how the two groups interact. A companion figure that had drawn a single producer lane for eight rounds, contradicting the project's own pre-registration, now separates the two stamping threads. (3) The word interval is retired for the timing sense and flight defined in its place, ahead of its first use. (4) Mode B is generalised: the failure is a quantum destroying a sample, of which the OpenMessaging Benchmark's positivity guard is one mechanism. An audit of the harnesses practitioners actually run — SPECjms2007, the Kafka bundled tools, RabbitMQ PerfTest, nats bench and Redpanda rpk — records what each does about resolution and sign. (5) The 1/D law is stated where it is argued: the displacement is a scheduling quantity and does not grow because a message travelled further, so the relative error falls as 1/T, and two identical systems whose clients stamp in different places are separated by the difference of their lags. The exposure curve now reaches below the crossover at which the displacement exceeds the path it is a correction to — which is where published sub-millisecond broker medians sit — and the curve is stated to apply to acknowledgment-referenced spans only, a harness that subtracts a send stamp being off it entirely. (6) One estimate changed. Unlike v2.6, this release moves a number: ρ(D, A) was computed from a variance identity on three separately binned, edge-truncated margins, did not conserve, and was not bounded — returning |ρ| > 1 on five of seventy conditions. It is now a windowed Pearson correlation on paired co-moments, with excluded pairs counted rather than dropped in silence. (7) Author biographies; the manuscript held at twelve pages with the displaced material in a supplement that grew to 49; and every quantity in the exposure discussion moved out of the prose and into the emitter, so the sentence a reader quotes and the table it summarises can no longer disagree. The test suite is now 3,866 tests at 100% branch coverage, up from 3,650.

The archive contains the instrumentation, every campaign script and ledger, the analysis suite that recomputes the manuscript's numbers from committed data and fails if paper and data disagree, and the three manuscript files: the paper, its supplementary material and the postmortem. A SHA256SUMS manifest lists every file in the archive so any single file can be verified independently of the zip.

Data note. No StatsBomb event data is redistributed. Replay plans derived from it are excluded from this record and regenerable byte-for-byte from a pinned upstream commit with the included scripts.
